claims.overstatement: None material; 'as they reported it' correctly marks self-report. Small wording point: in the source 'requested' applies to toxicology testing, while the autopsy item is that more autopsies were performed (35%); the claim's elliptical '58% said they requested more toxicology testing and 35% more autopsies' can be read as requested autopsies.
claims.note: Checks: 28/48 = 58.3% and 17/48 = 35.4%, shares of all 48 respondents (40% of the 120 elected coroners) answering how drug overdose death investigations had changed since the 2012 law. No measured testing or autopsy rates and no death counts. The paper's own summary is stronger than its table: the Discussion says about one-half reported increases in both testing and autopsy requests and the Conclusion says most reported more testing through more autopsy referrals, against 35.4% reporting more autopsies (over 26% reported all four changes); the claim rightly uses the table figures. The authors judge uptake of the mandate incomplete.

anchors.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, All respondents (n = 48) row
anchors.extracted: Asked whether drug overdose death investigations had changed since the 2012 testing law: yes 28 of 48 (58.3%). How they changed (all 48): more investigations 23 (47.9%); higher case load 19 (39.6%); more toxicology testing requested 28 (58.3%; text 'almost 60%'); more autopsies performed 17 (35.4%; text 35%); over 26% reported all four (data not shown).

anchors.locator: Methods › Study Population, 1st paragraph; Methods › Survey Design and Administration, 1st-2nd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Population: the 120 elected Kentucky coroners (deputies excluded); e-mail addresses found for 105; web survey sent in four stages, 5 April to 31 May 2016; 48 respondents, response rate 40%.

Kentucky law of 2012 required coroners and medical examiners to do post-mortem toxicology testing where the cause of death is unknown; expanded in 2015 to all decedents for whom a coroner investigation is required, with enhanced coroner training on drug-poisoning death investigation and certification.

After the mandate, 38% (18 of 48) said they always rely on toxicology results to determine the cause of a suspected overdose death and 25% always on autopsy findings; 62.5% (30 of 48) always use toxicology results to complete the death certificate and 41.7% (20) always to inform state agencies (Eastern region 22.7% vs other regions 57.7%, p = 0.0144).

anchors.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 3, Not Enough Financial Resources rows
anchors.extracted: System factors coroners said affected their decision to request an autopsy: availability of toxicology results without an autopsy report 76%, limited financial resources 31.2% (15 of 48; Eastern region 50% vs other regions 15.4%, p = 0.0099), distance to the regional medical examiner office 29%.

anchors.locator: Limitations, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph; Conclusion, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Authors note selection bias (non-respondents may differ) and that respondents may have presented themselves as complying with the law. Their Discussion summarises about one-half reporting increases in both toxicology and autopsy requests, and the Conclusion says most reported more testing through more autopsy referrals, both stronger than Table 2 (35.4% more autopsies).

claims.overstatement: None. 'Held another job' matches the source's concurrent positions (98%). The survey covers coroners only: it has no medical-examiner comparison and no death-record data, so it describes who certifies in Kentucky, not whether counts differ by system.
claims.note: Checks: 47 of 48 = 97.9% (text 98%; Table 1 'None' 1, 2.1%); funeral directors 28 of 48 = 58.3%. Reporting points not affecting this claim: the text lists law enforcement 13% among concurrent positions but Table 1 has no such row and its rows sum to 48; Table 1 gives 20 respondents with under ten years' service and 27 with ten or more, while Tables 2-4 label the groups the other way round (n = 27 and n = 20); Table 4's paraphernalia row repeats the toxicology row's values exactly.

anchors.extracted: 120 Kentucky coroners, a county office set in the state constitution; elected by county residents for four-year terms; eligibility: age 24, county resident for one year before the election and state resident for two years; no specific training in medicine or forensic pathology required.

Kentucky coroners need no medical training; most are not employed full time and many are funeral directors; newly elected coroners must complete a 40-hour basic death investigation training; coroners and deputies take annual continuing education (mandated for deputies, incentivised for elected coroners).

anchors.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1, Types of Concurrent Positions Held
anchors.extracted: Of 48 respondents, 2% served only as coroner (Table 1: none 1, 2.1%) and 98% held concurrent positions: funeral director 28 (58.3%), healthcare professional (physician, paramedic, EMT) 12 (25.0%), other 7 (14.6%); the text also lists law enforcement 13%, absent from Table 1.

Kentucky has a hybrid system: elected county coroners investigate and legally certify cause and manner of death for coroner cases, including drug poisonings; regional medical examiner offices give autopsy services and help interpret toxicology; the state office funds all toxicology; coroners may certify with or without an autopsy within ten days, and may collect samples, interpret the results and decide cause and manner themselves.

Second-hand (ref. 5, Warner et al., 2013): about 25% of US drug-poisoning death certificates in 2010 named no specific drug; states with centralized medical examiner systems had a higher share of certificates naming drugs than states with decentralized coroner systems; no figures given here.

Coroner-reported barriers to listing the specific drugs on death certificates: not enough room 83%, hospital stay between overdose and death 73%, toxicology results lag 54%, no requirement to list the drugs 47% (Eastern region 75% vs other regions 24%). Self-report, no medical-examiner comparison.
